headline: Nvidia's abrupt CEO exit, a violent Treasury selloff on Fed rate-hike bets and a surprisingly resilient equity tape set up a heavy week, with Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings next. Private capital keeps backing biotech and health deals, while central bankers press their warnings on private credit.

paragraphs.text: The biggest healthcare financing is Pfizer's deal with Blackstone Life Sciences, which commits up to $1.5 billion toward development of berobenatide, the monthly GLP-1 shot it inherited through Metsera. STAT notes Pfizer spent up to $10 billion on Metsera last year and is now bringing in private equity to help carry the cost. BioPharma Dive says the money backs a sprawling Phase 3 program. For investors, big pharma is again sharing late-stage risk with outside capital rather than carrying it all on the balance sheet.

paragraphs.text: Biotech capital markets were mixed. Windward priced a $175 million IPO to advance China-licensed lung drugs, but Endpoints reports Rezera postponed a planned $200 million IPO shortly before its debut, citing current market conditions. Private rounds continued: Neurosterix raised $105 million for a schizophrenia drug, and Fierce lists China's Eli Radiopharma at $60 million. Zus Health raised $33 million for AI clinical infrastructure, MedHaul $4.1 million, and Yicura BioMed closed a first Series B tranche led by Gobi Partners. Norwest closed a $4 billion multi-stage fund aimed at healthcare, biotech and AI, which is dry powder for the sector.

paragraphs.text: On pipelines and licensing, BioNTech paid $205 million for an FDA voucher from Scholar Rock, and Vor Bio paid RemeGen $10 million upfront for ex-China rights to a long-acting autoimmune asset. Kyverna dropped a next-generation CAR-T as it pursues approval of its lead therapy. Regeneron reported positive phase 2 data in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and plans a potentially pivotal trial in the first half of 2027. Bristol Myers merged its R&D divisions under Cristian Massacesi, and research chief Robert Plenge is leaving, ahead of a patent cliff according to Endpoints. Lilly won China's first oral GLP-1 weight-loss approval, ahead of Novo, per Fierce. Merck KGaA raised guidance for the third time this year but took a €366 million impairment tied to its CDMO sale to Lonza. PharmaLogic is buying Lantheus' CDMO business as Curium's acquisition of Lantheus advances.

paragraphs.text: Policy is the less comfortable story. Reuters, via Fierce and STAT, says the FDA has shelved the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher pilot, though the agency still says it is running. It also appears to have paused publishing complete response letters. BioPharma Dive says the agency has more than 1,000 open jobs and that the shortage is hitting industry. STAT asks whether Heidi Overton has the votes to run the FDA. HHS announced new psychedelics funding, including $4.9 million from ARPA-H for ibogaine in veteran PTSD. With Democrats taking control of Congress, Fierce Pharma says industry should expect heavier scrutiny of the administration's most-favored-nation pricing deals, and the NYT asks whether Democrats will pursue Kennedy or work with him.

UnitedHealth released an independent audit that found minor issues in how it develops medical policies, though Healthcare Dive notes it did not assess how criteria are applied in denials. Bon Secours Mercy raised its offer for a majority stake in Surgery Partners to a $6 billion valuation. Hospitals are bracing for Medicaid work rules taking effect January 1. paragraphs.text: Rates led the day. The FT says Treasuries are headed for their worst week since last year's tariff-driven rout after hotter inflation and hawkish Fed remarks hit investors who thought the bond rout was over. MarketWatch calls it the biggest yield surge since 2022 and links the volatility to Fed Chair Warsh's quiet communication style. New York Fed President Williams said inflation remains too high and more work is needed. WSJ reports European yields following Treasuries higher and the dollar at a 19-month high on bets for further Fed hikes. Today's U.S. inflation data is the next test. The Fed also announced that its October 2027 meeting will be a strategy session with no rate vote or statement, which the NYT frames as a first step in Warsh's broader plan to change how the central bank operates. Housing shows the strain: existing-home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, and jobless claims came in at 200,000 against 195,000 expected.

paragraphs.text: Equities proved resilient. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday after a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy, and the FT reports shares largely recovered by Thursday's close as investors bought the dip. The NYT says stocks logged their best week in months as AI shares broadly rose, though futures were lower this morning and Asia's tech rebound faded. Fallout continues: the FT reports a deeper Chinese AI sell-off on fears of tougher chip curbs, and Beijing warned Washington against using the affair as a pretext. Senator Scott asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick to testify, and CNBC says the political backdrop for next week's Trump-Xi summit has shifted. The FT and WSJ describe Colette Kress and new chair Harvey Jones now steering Nvidia, though earlier MarketWatch coverage still framed a CEO search. Analysts are split: Stephanie Link sold, while Freedom Capital's Meeks called the valuation too cheap, and William Blair upgraded AMD. Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO come next week.

paragraphs.text: Strategists are recalibrating. Citi says earnings beats are shrinking, which it reads as healthier. Goldman expects earnings growth to nearly halve across major indices in 2027 but says much of that is priced in. HSBC's global CIO says investors still underestimate AI and the real challenge is diversification. Microsoft's severe outage of Outlook, Teams and other services was still being repaired this morning, and the company says it was not malicious or cyber activity. Richemont posted 13% sales growth at constant exchange rates and a 39% first-half net profit rise. Asics shares slid as sales growth slowed, and Aviva reported higher premiums and a 29% rise in wealth inflows.

paragraphs.text: In commodities, the IEA says the oil market returns to surplus this quarter for the first time since the Iran war began as Gulf exports recover, though stockpiles will take months to rebuild. Iraq's October output was its highest since 2019. Prices still swing on U.S.-Iran headlines, and European stocks turned positive as oil dropped. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time since August and is heading for a sixth weekly loss. Elsewhere, the BoE is not expected to move in December despite solid growth, the PBOC kept an accommodative stance, a BOJ member urged caution on hikes, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico.

paragraphs.text: Coverage was heavy on regulatory warnings and light on actual defaults or ratings actions, so this is mostly a story about scrutiny. Bloomberg reports Bank of England Governor Bailey warning that private credit and stablecoins pose risks beyond their size, with few details in the headline. The NAIC's fall meeting will take up private credit as insurer exposure tops $1.2 trillion, per InsuranceNewsNet. The IAIS offered a calmer view, saying the shift toward alternative capital and private credit is not yet systemically concerning.

paragraphs.text: Australia's ASIC said it is fed up with the private credit sector's seeming indifference to cleaning up its act, according to ABC. Against that, an Ares executive told the South China Morning Post that Asia's private credit market has ample room to expand, so managers still see growth even as regulators press on conduct. The Banker says Austria's central bank has saved millions by using Chinese AI to analyse private credit, with no further detail here. In the UK, the FCA proposed more investment flexibility for workplace pensions, which could widen pools of capital open to alternatives.

paragraphs.text: The rate move is the main market-wide credit concern. FT Alphaville argues the bond market is starting to choke on AI debt, with too few baskets for so many large eggs. WSJ reports the AI trade dominated Treasuries for a month. With yields surging, the cost of financing for AI buildouts and leveraged borrowers is the thing to watch, though the list offers no spreads or issuance figures to measure it. The FT's opinion pages also warn about tokenisation and hyper-liquid shocks, and an HYG page appeared in the feed without any news content.

paragraphs.text: The IPO calendar centers on Anthropic. Seeking Alpha says demand is surging, and Interactive Brokers opened applications to retail clients across nine European markets. Reuters and WSJ both flag the offering, alongside Nvidia's results, as a test for the AI trade. Dangote's refinery IPO also drew interest: Bloomberg reports Africa's biggest money manager and Nigerian pension administrators applied for almost $1 billion of shares, citing people familiar. Not every listing is working. Bloomberg says investors are nursing losses from an IPO linked to an arms billionaire, with few details in the headline. Hong Kong's watchdog told banks to keep issuers out of IPO allocations. XTPL raised $6.53 million in post-IPO equity, with a Taiwanese fund taking nearly half. RedBird is exploring a listing for a new AC Milan holding company housing its sports and entertainment investments.

Reuters Breakingviews says UK bank M&A will happen but slowly, and the City's new Lord Mayor is pushing to get UK pension savings invested at home. Banking Dive also reports BofA is settling a class action over allegedly unauthorized accounts opened from 2012 to 2023, and the Fed announced an enforcement action against a former United Community Bank employee.
